postTitle: When the Default Plan Doesn't Fit You
topic: Same pension, two partners: in many schemes a spouse is the default and an unmarried partner has to be named

assumptions.notes: One illustrative workplace pension of €80,000. Two employees with the same pension, each with a partner of fifteen years; one couple married, one not. Many schemes pay a survivor benefit or lump sum to a legal spouse by default; failing a spouse, many pay the estate, which follows inheritance rules. Rules vary by scheme and country. No other figures.

routeStory.disclosure: Illustrative. Rules vary by scheme and country.

hookVariants.narration: Same eighty thousand euro pension. In many schemes, a spouse is paid by default. An unmarried partner has to be named.
Fifteen years together can count for nothing on one pension form.
Do you know who your pension pays if you die? Most people have never read that rule.

beats.narration: Two people. Same job, same eighty thousand euro pension, both with a partner of fifteen years. One couple is married. One is not.
Read the scheme rules, not the brochure. Many say: if a member dies, pay the spouse.
For the married employee, that default does roughly the right thing.
For the unmarried one, it fails. Many schemes then pay the estate, and inheritance rules may leave the partner out entirely.
The fix is often one free form. A beneficiary designation, naming the partner.
Where a scheme will not accept it, the workaround is a will, plus life cover the partner owns.
beats.subtext: A will, plus life cover they own

beats.narration: So for every account that pays out, ask three questions. Who does it pay by default? Who is named today? And will the scheme accept my choice?
